atoms.b: Before the ((++Romans Ottomans)) came to Britain, people had quite simple ways of staying clean. Most Britons washed in rivers and ((++streams showers)).

Romans brought new ((++hygiene hydrogen)) practices to Britain. Large public baths were built in towns and cities, while ((++wealthy poor)) Romans sometimes even had smaller private baths in their homes.

atoms.text: Archaeologists have discovered many Roman bathhouses across Britain. One of the best-preserved Roman bath complexes is located in the appropriately-named city of Bath in South West England.
Back then, the city was called Aquae Sulis or “the Waters of Sulis”. It was named after a local Celtic goddess associated with healing and thermal springs.
atoms.sound: Back then, the city was called Aquae Soolis or “the Waters of Soolis”. It was named after a local Celtic goddess associated with healing and thermal springs.

instruction.text: Fill in the gaps in this conversation between a Roman and a Briton at a public bath.

atoms.b: Wow, this public bath is incredible. You ((++Romans Egyptians)) really know how to keep clean!
We don’t just use it to stay clean! It’s ((++also only)) a place where people meet and socialise.
Can you tell me more about how the ((++baths markets)) work?

We have three main rooms; each with a different ((++temperature miniature)). We start in the tepidarium, which is nice and warm — perfect for spending time with our ((++friends pets)), gossiping and hearing the latest news!

After we are nice and relaxed, we go into the heat of the caldarium to ((++sweat sweet)) everything out. We finish in the frigidarium, which has ((++cold hot)) water to cool down. It’s a real spa experience!
I didn’t know that going to have a bath could be such a ((++fun boring)) day out!
